summary: Newton's Third Law for ages 12–13: every force is one half of an interaction between TWO objects — if A pushes or pulls B, then B pushes or pulls A with an equal-magnitude, opposite-direction force of the same type. The decisive learner moves are to name the two different bodies in each pair, to see the pair stays equal even during acceleration and for very different masses, and to distinguish a third-law pair (two bodies) from balanced forces on one body. This is the hardest of Newton's laws; the central misconception is fusing a third-law pair with balanced forces on a single object and concluding they 'cancel'. Frame the law as one simultaneous interaction, not sequential 'action then reaction'.
misconceptions: Pairing the two forces on the SAME body and concluding they cancel — conflating a third-law pair with balanced forces (the central error; Taber)
During acceleration the 'active' pusher exerts the bigger force ('Blue pushes Green harder to start the motion') — reported in ~100% of incoming students and very stubborn
The more massive object exerts more force (forces are equal; different EFFECTS come from different masses)
'Action' then 'reaction' implies a time sequence (B responds after A), rather than simultaneous forces
Third-law forces 'cancel out' (they act on different bodies, so can never cancel on one body)
Greater difficulty identifying the partner force in gravitational interactions than in contact pushes

activities.title: Matched force-meters: the pair stays equal
steps: Set two carts nose-to-nose with a push–pull force sensor on the front of each, touching (ordinary spring newton-meters only measure pulls; if that is all you have, hook two together and have one cart tow the other instead), and predict, before pushing, what each sensor will read when one cart pushes gently and when it pushes hard.
Make one cart push the other and read both sensors; then push harder and read again; then keep pushing so both carts speed up together, and read the sensors while they are accelerating.
Record whether the two readings are ever different, including while the carts are speeding up.
State in your own words which object each measured force acts on.
activities.insight: The two forces in an interaction are always equal in magnitude, even while the objects accelerate and even when one is doing the 'pushing' — so there is no 'stronger pusher'.

activities.title: Find the partner: two bodies, never the same one
steps: Watch a skater shove a wall and recoil, or push off a wall yourself, and name the two forces: the force on the wall and the force on the skater.
For each named force, apply the 'swap and reverse' test: if 'A acts on B', its partner is 'B acts on A' — state it aloud.
Use a highlight tool (optional) that greys out everything except the partner force on the OTHER body, and check it lands on a different object.
Decide whether the two forces in a pair could ever cancel each other, and explain why or why not.
activities.insight: A third-law pair always consists of forces on two different objects, so the pair can never cancel on a single object.

activities.title: Equal forces, unequal effects (bug vs windscreen)
steps: Consider a collision between a light object and a heavy object (e.g. a bug and a windscreen, or a small car and a truck); predict which experiences the bigger force.
Using a mass control (optional dial) or by reasoning, compare the forces on the two objects and then compare their accelerations.
Explain, using F = ma, why the lighter object changes its motion much more while the forces are equal.
Write one sentence separating 'which force is bigger' (neither — they're equal) from 'which object is affected more' (the lighter one).
activities.insight: Equal interaction forces produce different effects on different masses; the different accelerations come from the different masses (via F = ma), not from unequal forces (how much damage is done also depends on how fragile each object is).

activities.title: Book, table and Earth: pair vs balanced
steps: Draw or reveal the three bodies in a book-on-table scene: Earth, book, table.
List the forces acting ON the book (its weight from the Earth, and the table's upward push) and state that these two balance because the book is at rest.
For the book's weight, find its third-law partner by the swap test (the book's gravitational pull up on the Earth).
For the table's push on the book, find its partner (the book's push down on the table).
Sort every named force into 'balanced forces on one body' versus 'third-law pair across two bodies', and check each pair is the same TYPE of force (both gravitational, or both contact).
activities.insight: The two forces on the book balance (same body) but are NOT a pair; each force's genuine partner acts on a different body and is the same type of force.

activities.title: Socratic 'am I pulling you?' questioning
steps: With a partner or an in-role tutor, pull on opposite ends of a metre rule and answer: Which way am I pulling you? Which way are you pulling me?
Answer: Can I pull you without you pulling me back?
Relate your answers to the rule that the interaction is simultaneous — not 'my pull first, then your pull'.
Restate the law without using the words 'action' and 'reaction', using 'A on B' and 'B on A' instead.
activities.insight: Interaction forces are simultaneous and mutual; the 'action then reaction' wording wrongly implies a time order.

activities.title: Retrieval: sort pairs, match partners, apply
steps: Match each named force to its partner on the OTHER body (e.g. 'rocket pushes gas down' ↔ 'gas pushes rocket up').
Categorise given force-pairs as 'third-law pair' or 'balanced forces on one body'.
Answer the book-on-table item: which forces form third-law pairs (there is more than one pair), and how do you decide?
For rocket propulsion and gun recoil, name both forces and the object each acts on.
activities.insight: Learners can reliably identify third-law partners (different object, same type) and separate them from balanced forces across varied contexts.

checkQuestion: A book rests on a table. One student says: 'The table pushing up on the book and the book pushing down on the table are a Newton's Third Law pair.' Another says: 'No — the pair to the table's push up on the book is the book's WEIGHT.' Who is right, and how do you decide which two forces form a Third Law pair?
checkAnswer: The first student is right. A Third Law pair is two forces of the SAME type acting on DIFFERENT objects: the table pushes up on the book and the book pushes down on the table. The book's weight (Earth pulling the book) acts on the SAME object as the table's push — the book — so those two are BALANCED forces, not a pair; weight's actual pair is the book pulling the Earth up. To find a pair: state 'A acts on B', and its pair is always 'B acts on A' (same type, different objects).
